In the principalities of central Java there is the celuring-set ensemble, which strikes bronze bowls shaped like half a coconut with iron bars. In the West the singing bowl entered New Age music from the early 1970s, for example Henry Wolff and Nancy Hennings' album Tibetan Bells and its successors; it also appears in music therapy, sound healing and yoga.

Its vibration has both radial and tangential components, and unstable modes cause beating; with a hard mallet, light pressure and high speed a wobble or a broken, fragmented tone may appear. Partly filling it with water changes the tuning, and the source gives no clear range. Unlike a gong, the greatest vibration is concentrated at the open rim; Buddhist ritual mostly uses striking and not the sustained frictional tone.
此類立鐘起源於中國，近年以『磬』稱之；青銅鐘可上溯商代（公元前十六至十一世紀），: Standing bells of this kind originated in China and have been called the qing in recent times; bronze bells go back to the Shang dynasty (16th to 11th century BC), and the early nao was a cup shape with a hollow handle, mouth upward, struck on the outer wall with a mallet, usually a single example in the south and a set of three in the north. After Buddhism spread between the 2nd and 7th centuries AD the making of large ritual bells took off, and China also used cast iron. The singing bowl that can sustain a tone is thought to be a modern phenomenon; Tibetan sources do not record it, and those sold as Tibetan ritual instruments mostly come from North India or Nepal. It reached the West in the early 1970s and was used in music in 1972, and it has since become a common instrument in New Age music.

The qing (ritual implement), also called the standing bell or resting bell, originated in China. It is an inverted bell, supported from below with the rim facing up, usually bowl-shaped, and it ranges in size from a few centimetres to a metre. It is played by striking, and some can be called singing bowls, where a suede-wrapped mallet is drawn around the outer rim to produce a sustained tone; it usually rests on a cushion, and a small one can be held lightly in the hand. It is an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 133.2. Besides musical performance it appears in Buddhist meditation and chanting, and in relaxation, personal spirituality, music therapy, sound healing and yoga.
磬（法器）的基本操作是先將碗形鐘倒置、口緣朝上，由下方支撐；通常置於枕墊上，讓口: The basic handling of the qing is to turn the bowl-shaped bell over, rim upward, supported from below; it normally rests on a cushion so that the rim can vibrate freely, and a small one can be held lightly in the hand. It sounds in two ways: striking the outside with a mallet for a bell tone, or drawing a wooden or suede-wrapped mallet around the outer rim so that friction produces a sustained tone, its volume changing with speed and pressure. Partly filling it with water adjusts the pitch.
